nameStory: The Pruinose Squash Bee gets its name from its special relationship with squash plants - it's completely devoted to visiting squash, pumpkin, and gourd flowers for pollen. The word 'pruinose' means having a frosted or powdery appearance, referring to the bee's coating of pale, dusty-looking hairs that give it a slightly frosted look.
description: This medium-sized solitary bee is a black-bodied specialist that lives for squash blossoms. About half an inch long, it has a distinctive black body decorated with whitish bands across its fuzzy abdomen and a coating of yellowish hairs all over. Unlike honeybees that live in hives, each female digs her own underground nest near squash plants. You'll most often spot these busy bees early in the morning, frantically collecting the large, sticky pollen from squash flowers before the blossoms close by noon.

idTips.label: Squash flower obsession
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on squash, pumpkin, and gourd flowers - if you see a bee on these blossoms in your garden, it's likely this species

idTips.label: Black body with white bands
idTips.description: Jet black body with distinct whitish stripes across the abdomen that contrast sharply with the dark background

idTips.label: Yellowish fuzzy coating
idTips.description: Entire body covered in soft, yellowish hairs that give it a slightly dusty or frosted appearance when viewed up close

idTips.label: Medium size
idTips.description: About half an inch long (11-14mm) - noticeably larger than a honeybee but smaller than a bumble bee

idTips.label: Early morning activity
idTips.description: Most active in early morning hours when squash flowers are open, becoming less visible as flowers close before noon

idTips.label: Ground nesting behavior
idTips.description: Females can be seen entering and exiting small holes in bare soil near squash plants, often with small mounds of dirt at the entrance

habitat: Look for these bees in vegetable gardens, farms, and anywhere squash family plants grow - from backyard pumpkin patches to community gardens. They prefer areas with loose, well-drained soil for nesting, often choosing spots that have been recently disturbed by gardening or irrigation. You'll also find them around wild gourds in field edges and disturbed areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring when early squash plantings start to flower. Look for females starting to dig nests in garden soil.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity during main squash growing season - best time to observe them. Most easily spotted on squash blossoms in early morning hours before 10 AM.
seasonality.fall: Still active on late-season squash and pumpkin flowers. New generation may emerge for autumn cucurbit blooms before overwintering underground.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off and the species overwinters as developing larvae in underground nests, completely invisible until next growing season.

funFact: These bees are such extreme squash specialists that their entire life cycle is timed to squash flowers - they wake up when the flowers open at dawn and practically race against time to collect pollen before the blossoms slam shut by noon, making them nature's most punctual pollinators!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other dark bees visiting squash flowers, but the Pruinose Squash Bee's dedication to cucurbit flowers is nearly absolute - other bees will visit many flower types while these stick almost exclusively to their squash obsession. Memory trick: if it's on a squash flower, it's probably a squash bee!
contextualKnowledge: There's some naming confusion around squash bees - this species is sometimes called the Eastern Cucurbit Bee, and the name 'squash bee' can refer to several different species. The scientific name has also changed over time, with some sources listing it as Peponapis pruinosa instead of Xenoglossa pruinosa.
compareHints: Since this is the only Xenoglossa species commonly found in New England, compare it to other bees in squash flowers. Unlike honeybees which are smaller and more golden, or bumble bees which are much larger and rounder, squash bees have that distinctive black-and-white banded pattern. They're also much more single-minded about staying on cucurbit flowers compared to other bee species that flower-hop throughout the garden.
